scope: The cookbook's rules for requirement keywords in its own artifacts: which normative keywords a rule uses (RFC 2119 / RFC 8174, BCP 14), in which case they carry their defined meaning, how a requirement with no keyword is read, how a rule's keyword sets the severity of a lint finding when an artifact fails the check that rule states, and which severities block /approve-artifact. Out of scope: the named-rule bullet form and the formatting topics' own checks.
research_type: How-to / troubleshooting (intent Do; domain technical writing; method practitioner and standards sources). Bar: How-to / troubleshooting, no escalation (owner ruling Q13).

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient, go to authoritative sources first (the standards bodies that define normative keywords: IETF RFC 2119, RFC 8174, RFC 7322; W3C QA Framework and Manual of Style; WHATWG Infra; OASIS; ISO/IEC Directives Part 2; ETSI), then the tools' own documentation (ReSpec, Bikeshed, idnits, Vale, ESLint, markdownlint, SARIF, GitHub code scanning), then practitioner and editor views (W3C spec-prod list, W3C wiki, plainlanguage.gov); corroborate across independent publishers; record provenance at generation time.
methodology.search_strategy: WebSearch and WebFetch for each standard's own text (rfc-editor.org plain-text RFCs, w3.org TR and guide pages, infra.spec.whatwg.org, oasis-open.org, portal.etsi.org), each tool's own documentation page on severity and exit codes, the idnits source on ietf-tools GitHub, and the W3C spec-prod mailing-list thread on RFC 2119 styling. Queries named the topic only.
methodology.inclusion: Primary standards text and tool documentation that state keyword meaning, keyword case, conformance boilerplate, finding severity or exit/merge behaviour; editor statements from named standards editors on public archives.
methodology.exclusion: Pages not fetched; blog summaries restating RFC 2119 without adding anything; current ISO/IEC Directives on iso.org (403, not fetched); the KAN and ETSI NGSI-LD pages (404).
methodology.scoring: guidelines/researching/evidence/verification-and-trust-scoring: Authority 30 + Independent corroboration 25 + Accuracy/verifiability 20 + Currency 10 + Transparency 15; domain bar How-to / troubleshooting (LOW-MEDIUM, broad independent consensus), no escalation.

summary: The keyword definitions hold: RFC 2119 makes MUST/MUST NOT absolute, SHOULD/SHOULD NOT a recommendation whose implications must be weighed before deviating, and MAY truly optional (ISO/IEC Annex H agrees in its shall/should/may forms). Three rules are stronger than the sources: no standard requires keywords for every requirement (RFC 8174 says normative text does not require them), so 'MUST use RFC 2119 keywords' (gf-rfc-keywords, conventions.md and the artifact-formatting rule) is supported only at SHOULD, paired with a MUST to say how keywordless text is read (W3C QA Framework Requirement 7). The 'bold or uppercase' rule is contradicted in its bold alternative: under RFC 8174 the words carry BCP 14 meaning only in all capitals, and OASIS likewise ties the meaning to UPPERCASE. The severity rules hold: across Vale, ESLint, markdownlint, Bikeshed and GitHub code scanning only error-level findings fail the run or the merge check, warnings do not, which supports approve-on-zero-fail and a MUST-to-error, SHOULD-to-warning, MAY-to-no-finding mapping (an inference; no source states it directly). The topic is missing: uppercase-only meaning; flagging lowercase keywords in rule text; stating the keyword interpretation (the BCP 14 boilerplate); stating how keywordless text is read; no keywords in non-normative text; one keyword per requirement in subject-keyword-operation form; the core keyword subset; no 'MUST not'/'MAY NOT'; one keyword set never mixed; keywords only where actually required.
open_questions: Case convention: follow RFC 8174 (only all-capital keywords carry meaning) or WHATWG Infra's willful violation (lowercase keywords carry the same meaning and are preferred for legibility); the sources support either if declared, and the owner chooses one.

Whether skipping a SHOULD requires a documented reason (follow-must-address-should-checks) or only that the implications be understood and weighed (RFC 2119's wording); RFC 2119 does not require documentation.
Whether warnings ever block /approve-artifact (an ESLint --max-warnings style threshold) or never do; the tools make a warning threshold optional and default to warnings not blocking.
Whether rules restrict themselves to the five keywords MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY (as Infra encourages) or also admit SHALL, REQUIRED, RECOMMENDED and OPTIONAL as BCP 14 defines them.
Whether a lowercase keyword found in rule text is reported as a WARN (as Bikeshed's opt-in accidental-2119 lint and ReSpec's warnings do) or a FAIL.
Whether lint-artifact's GF-03 level 'WARN if missing' stays a warning; the sources support a keyword as SHOULD, which maps to a warning, but the owner decides.

Whether keywords are additionally styled (bold, or the W3C Manual of Style's em with class rfc2119) for readability; no source makes styling carry the meaning, and a W3C editor recommends dropping the formatting requirement.
limitations: The current ISO/IEC Directives Part 2 on iso.org returned 403; Annex H is quoted from the 2004 edition as archived on an IETF mailing list (mhonarc.org), so its wording may differ from the current edition.
The W3C Manual of Style states it holds no requirements (they are in W3C pubrules); pubrules and specberus were not fetched, so no W3C publication requirement on keyword styling is cited.

No source directly states a mapping from a requirement keyword to a lint severity; keyword-sets-finding-severity is inferred from RFC 2119's definitions, the SARIF levels, the QA Framework's HTTP/1.1 conformance example and the linters' error/warning behaviour.
The ESLint, markdownlint, Vale, GitHub, OASIS and ETSI pages carry no publication date and are cited as n.d.; the vale.sh pages are rendered from GitBook.
Expert views come from one W3C mailing-list thread (spec-prod, May-June 2023); no linter maintainer was found writing on mapping requirement levels to severities.
